talks.title: Yuval Gorchover: From Notebook Chaos to Production Gold (HE) | PyData Tel Aviv 2025
talks.description:
A model’s performance in a notebook is a promise; production is where that promise is often broken. This is "Notebook Chaos": the silent killer of ML systems where real-world predictions fail because features diverge between training and serving.

This session follows the story of Sarah, a data scientist deploying a churn prediction model. We'll diagnose why her high-performing notebook model fails in production, identifying the two root causes: feature translation drift and late-arriving data.

Having established the problem, we’ll introduce the solution: an open-source feature store (Feast). We will explore the core concepts that bridge the gap from research to production, including:

* "A Layer, Not a Platform": How a feature store integrates with your *existing* data stack (like Snowflake and Redis) without vendor lock-in.
* Point-in-Time Correctness: How to automatically prevent data leakage for training.
* Online/Offline Stores: A clear-eyed look at managing data for both training and low-latency inference.

You will leave with a clear, practical blueprint for implementing a production-grade feature management system.

Speaker Bio:
Yuval Gorchover is a lead the AI/ML Engineering team at Voyantis, translating between data scientists, engineers, and business folks. My philosophy? Find the simplest solution that actually delivers.
I write about this stuff for Towards Data Science and practice yoga when I'm not debugging pipelines.

Speakers:
Vinayak Nair

Description:
Vinayak Nair from LiveEO shares how his team built an end-to-end system to transform raw satellite imagery into analysis-ready datasets for vegetation monitoring, deforestation detection, and infrastructure monitoring. The talk covers their cloud-native pipeline that automates satellite data acquisition, storage, and preprocessing while handling various sensors and formats. Using Prefect for workflow orchestration and Anyscale Ray for distributed processing, they reduced processing times from days to near real-time. The system leverages the open-source STAC (SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog) standard for metadata indexing, enabling fast querying and long-term interoperability. Nair discusses practical challenges like inconsistent metadata, diverse sensor types, and provider API drift, while sharing lessons learned from processing 45.5 terabytes and 5.2 million items in production. The talk provides valuable insights into building flexible, scalable geospatial analytics systems that support AI workloads.

talks.title: Abbas Raza: Beyond the Demo: Shipping Computer-Use Agents in Production
talks.description:
Computer-use agents, AI systems that interact directly with browsers and graphical user interfaces, have rapidly moved from impressive demos to early production deployments. However, operating these agents reliably in real environments introduces a class of challenges that are often underestimated or ignored in early implementations. This talk presents a practical, experience-driven examination of computer-use agents deployed in live business workflows. It traces the evolution from low-level browser control approaches (e.g., DOM- and vision-based interaction) to higher-level abstractions and orchestration layers, highlighting the architectural tradeoffs that emerged only under real-world load, UI drift, and partial system failures. Key topics include: Common failure modes in computer-use agents, including UI volatility, non-deterministic model behavior, timing and synchronization issues, and brittle task decomposition Reliability strategies such as constrained action spaces, verification loops, retries and recovery, fallback paths, and human-in-the-loop controls Observability gaps unique to UI-driven agents and practical techniques for debugging, monitoring, and post-incident analysis Latency, cost, and throughput tradeoffs when scaling computer-use agents beyond isolated tasks Security, compliance, and blast-radius considerations when agents operate on live systems The talk also challenges the assumption that increased autonomy always leads to better outcomes, and proposes a more pragmatic model for deploying computer-use agents as constrained, inspectable systems rather than fully autonomous actors. Attendees will leave with a concrete mental model for evaluating when computer-use agents are appropriate, architectural patterns that improve reliability, and a set of anti-patterns to avoid when moving from demo to production.

Video Recorded at The AI Conference. Copyright, The AI Conference, All Rights Reserved

High-Throughput Data Pipelines: Optimizing data ingestion, preprocessing, labeling, and streaming from AV fleets to centralized data stores.  Resource-Efficient Training: Methods for managing infrastructure resources, minimizing overhead, and maximizing hardware utilization in hyperscale environments.  Real-Time Inference at Scale: Solutions for low-latency inference deployment, edge-to-cloud orchestration, and continuous model updates in large AV fleets. Human/Agent Co-Creation of Shared Knowledge with Semiont

Semiont is a new open-source framework from the AI Alliance that enables humans and intelligent agents to co-create shared knowledge — governed by you and built to last. At its core, Semiont supports the simultaneous co-creation of a wiki and a knowledge graph, allowing text and structured relationships to evolve side by side. On top of this foundation, Semiont provides powerful retrieval and contextualization, drawing on the principles of GraphRAG (Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation).
By weaving together collaborative editing with graph-grounded semantics, Semiont provides a durable framework for meaning-making that goes beyond static documentation or siloed AI memory. Humans and intelligent agents can jointly annotate, connect, and refine entities and relationships, while operators retain full control over what is shared and preserved.
In this talk, I will introduce the core principles behind Semiont, demonstrate its workflows, review its roadmap, and explore the broader implications for sustainable knowledge infrastructure in the age of AI.

talks.title: Adrian Kosowski | Keynote: Post-Transformer Frontier: More Intelligence per Watt, Token & Dollar
talks.description:
Transformers have reshaped AI, but they were never designed as a foundation for intelligence that must persist and grow over time. Today’s reasoning models often gain capability by generating and accumulating an ever-growing trace of reasoning tokens. This raises latency, drives up inference cost, and increases energy consumption. We are already seeing diminishing returns from scaling parameters and inference-time compute. This keynote explains why the next frontier in AI will come from architectural breakthroughs that produce more intelligence per watt, token, and dollar. I will map the emerging post-Transformer landscape across three architectural frontiers: persistent and recurrent memory, sparse and selective computation, and continual adaptation — and show how they need to come together to achieve this goal. I will then introduce BDH — an architecture that unifies memory, reasoning, and adaptation — and lay out a path beyond static parameters and ephemeral token histories toward AI systems that retain what matters, reason and adapt over long horizons, and improve through experience.

talks.title: Alina Solotarov, Fraunhofer: When Machines Imagine: Ethical Futures Beyond Human Design
talks.description:
Alina Solotarov, AI Ethicist and Futures Researcher, Fraunhofer

When Machines Imagine: Ethical Futures Beyond Human Design

As generative AI systems increasingly produce visions of the future—often without clear authorship or accountability—they raise urgent ethical questions that go beyond traditional frameworks. What does it mean when machines “imagine” on our behalf? What ethical obligations emerge when AI-generated images shape foresight, policy, and public imagination?

In this talk, Alina Solotarov draws from Futures Studies, Information Ethics, and real-world case studies of AI-generated images of the future (AIGIFs) to argue for a radical rethinking of ethical frameworks. Moving beyond compliance and control narratives, she introduces the concept of ethical co-imagination—an approach that integrates transparency, representational justice, and the epistemic integrity of visual foresight.

Drawing on her research at Fraunhofer ISI and her award-winning Master's thesis at Freie Universität Berlin, Alina offers a compelling synthesis of theory and practice. She examines how current frameworks—whether utilitarian, deontological, or regulatory—fail to account for the ontological and semantic ambiguities of machine-generated futures.

This session will equip thought leaders, technologists, and policymakers with fresh tools to evaluate and govern generative AI—not only in terms of harm reduction, but also in terms of who gets to imagine, what is left out, and how we build futures worth living in.

talks.title: Ankit Sobti: The Agentic OS: a first-principles approach to building agents that get things done
talks.description:
AI agents are remarkable. They've given us the ability to reason over complex, multi-dimensional knowledge and capabilities across an organization, and take actions at a scale that previously demanded far more time and resources. There is a meaningful gap, though, between agents that demo well (AI always demos well) and agents that actually move the needle. As the agentic discourse moves from models and frameworks to scaled deployment and ROI, the harder question is whether agents can survive contact with a real organization: real data, fragmented systems, ambiguous outcomes, and decisions that carry actual risk. This talk draws from our experience at Postman building and operating a family of 30+ AI agents in production across our enterprise organization. Integrations multiplied, context fragmented, and the emerging mesh of agents calling one another began to resemble the distributed-system architectures many of us spent the last decade learning to avoid. AI-native is not just about deploying more agents, and much more about making the business legible to them: domains, judgment, strategy, permissions, and outcomes.

As agents take on this kind of work, enterprise realities come into play — hybrid and on-prem environments, governance, security, and operational control all shape how these systems can operate responsibly at scale. As agents operate within these enterprise constraints, their workloads grow, and economics and model strategy become part of the architecture. talks.title: Arif Poonawala: How to win the battle for the user in the agentic age
talks.description:
The AI era looks like a fight over models, chips, and compute. The real fight is over the user. Whoever delivers the best experience wins the market, and agents are now the front line of that experience. Most agents are losing it. They launch blind to the people they serve and miss the moments that decide whether a user stays or leaves. The gap between shipping an agent and shipping one people actually rely on is product context: the behavioral and business signals that tell an agent when to step in, what to say, and whether it worked. This talk makes the case that the companies who win the age of AI won't be the ones with the most agents. They'll be the ones whose agents truly understand the user, and shows what it takes to build them.

talks.title: Art Gilliland: Move Fast and Don’t Break Things: A New Model for AI Governance
talks.description:
Every enterprise wants to move faster with AI, but most governance programs slow that down because they were built for humans, not machines. AI agents act in milliseconds, often with more access than any single task requires, and most governance programs lose sight of what they’re doing once they’re running. Companies often feel forced into a false choice: lock AI down and slow the business or move fast and lose control. The companies pulling ahead rejected that trade-off entirely. They rebuilt their controls to match the speed of AI, getting more agents into production faster, with a complete record of every action to back it up. This session shows how, and what becomes possible when authorization stops being a policy you set once and starts keeping pace with every decision your AI makes.

talks.title: Camila Maia: The Real Cost of Scaling AI: An Inference Playbook
talks.description:
Training gets the headlines, but inference pays the bills, and for most AI products, it's where margins are won or lost. Today, the vast majority of inference runs on big cloud providers or abstraction platforms, where convenience is high but cost visibility is low. Teams that carefully optimize their models often ship them on infrastructure chosen by default, then discover at scale that their fastest-growing cost is also their least understood. This session is a hands-on framework for understanding inference unit economics in practice. We'll start with the problem every team eventually faces: usage grows, the invoice grows faster, and nobody can quite explain the relationship between the two, because layers of managed abstraction hide the variables that drive cost. The core of the talk is a step-by-step method for making those variables visible. We'll break down how to calculate your true cost per request (not just the sticker price), why utilization — not hardware price — is the number that matters most, and how workload shape (batch vs. real-time, bursty vs. steady, token-heavy vs. compute-light) should drive infrastructure choices. And we'll challenge a common assumption along the way: GPUs aren't the only answer. A growing share of production inference runs efficiently on CPU-only servers, and knowing when that trade-off wins is part of the framework. With the model in hand, we'll map the decision landscape honestly: serverless APIs, managed GPU endpoints, dedicated GPU compute, and CPU-based inference each win in different scenarios, and attendees will get a simple break-even approach for knowing when to move between them. We'll close with a brief look at how these principles play out on dedicated infrastructure: one example of how teams that own their inference stack turn cost from a mystery into a lever. Attendees will walk away with a clear AI infra framework, a checklist for auditing their current inference spend, and a clear-eyed way to answer the question every engineering lead eventually gets asked: "why is our AI bill this high, and what are we doing about it?"

Video Recorded at The AI Conference. Copyright, The AI Conference, All Rights Reserved

talks.title: Carlos Acevedo: True Zero Data Retention Is Structural, Not a Clause in a Contract
talks.description:

This means Zero Data Retention is only enforceable up to your search vendor's boundary, unless it's a property of a vertically integrated stack. If they're calling an external index for some queries, then you can't guarantee true ZDR for your users. In this talk, you'll get practical advice for how to trace the retrieval path your queries actually take; how to verify end-to-end privacy; why agents are compounding this privacy gap; and three questions to take back to your team to ensure reliably enforceable ZDR across all endpoints without degradation in result quality.

talks.title: Chetan Conikee: Your agents' traces are your most valuable asset: reading the software factory floor
talks.description:
A modern harness does not click buttons. It writes a shell line, a pipe, an inline script, and hands it to an interpreter. It does that in step with one inference backend, the frontier model it was trained against and benchmarked with. Swap the harness and you have not measured efficiency; you have changed the model, the prompt cache, the tool vocabulary and the compaction rules at once. Olki sits beside the harness you already use—Codex and OpenCode—and records what actually ran. Each line becomes typed events, one per stage, with the program, its arguments, and what it touched. From that record, four readers get their own view: the organization across machines, the inference provider counting repeated failures and the cache that carries the bill, and the product owner asking how agents use the tool they shipped. This session walks the software factory floor: how your harness interacts with the inference provider stack, how a prefix cache lives, why turn two must reach turn one's node, what a subagent or a model switch costs, and what you can only learn by reading the record instead of swapping the harness.

As customer-facing GenAI support systems move from prototypes to production, reliability is no longer a nice-to-have—it’s a hard requirement. Securing Clinical Trust: Challenges in Evaluating and Monitoring Medical AI

As clinical AI systems become integral to patient care and healthcare operations, organizations’ AI Governance duty to prove that their systems are safe, effective, and legal require robust evaluation and continuous monitoring. This session covers:
Key challenges in effective evaluation of medical AI solutions include data contamination, fragile metrics, benchmarks that lack resemblance to real-world use cases, and the need for localize validation.
Legal requirements including national and state laws, regulations, industry standards, and contractual obligations that require bias, safety, and quality evaluation.
Medical red teaming gaps that must be addressed to uncover ethical, safety, and security vulnerabilities unique to healthcare applications.
Clinical cognitive biases such as anchoring, framing, and sycophancy that impact LLMs as well as humans and can skew AI‑driven recommendations.
MLOps requirements for continuous testing and monitoring, to ensure models remain safe, compliant, and clinically reliable as regulations and data drift evolve.
We’ll explore emerging open-source libraries like MedHELM and LangTest, new research datasets like MedSafetyBench and MedAgentBench, and evolving standards from CHAI and NIST aiming to help address these challenges. Today Cursor, Cognition, Harvey and others ship their own models, built on open weights and sharpened with reinforcement learning — not because they wanted to become model labs, but because prompting a general model was no longer good enough for their products. This talk traces how that shift happened and what it means for anyone building AI products. I'll cover the four preconditions that made it possible: open-weight models good enough to specialize, verifiable rewards that made RL practical outside a lab, agents that raised the bar from plausible answers to reliable task completion, and the economics of a small custom model beating a frontier API. I'll then look at how the vendor landscape has organized itself — who sells post-training today, and how much of the work each option leaves in your hands. Drawing on post-training Llama 3 and 4 at Meta, co-founding Eigen AI, and now leading AI training at Nebius, I'll share how we approach this at Nebius: an AI cloud where training tooling — both our own and our partners' — sits directly on the compute, so teams can post-train their own models without stitching together a stack. Safety by Design for Generative AI: Preventing Child Sexual Abuse

We are at a crossroads with generative artificial intelligence (generative AI). Generative AI is being misused today to further sexual harm against children. 1 in 10 minors report knowing peers that have used generative AI to create explicit images of other kids; 11% of reports of sexual extortion (in which tactics were apparent) to the National Center of Missing and Exploited Children, included threatening children with fake sexual imagery; 50% of Law Enforcement have encountered AI-generated child sexual abuse material used to groom minors; the Internet Watch Foundation observed a 10% increase in sadistic and hardcore AI-generated child sexual abuse material in the material they assessed from 2023 to 2024.

Yet, we find ourselves in a rare moment — a window of opportunity — to still go down the right path with generative AI and ensure children are protected as the technology is built. In a show of powerful collective action, some of the world’s most influential AI leaders have chosen to do just that. In collaboration with Thorn and All Tech Is Human: Amazon, Anthropic, Civitai, Google, Invoke, Meta, Metaphysic, Microsoft, Mistral AI, OpenAI, and Stability AI have publicly committed to Safety by Design principles. This responsible and ethical AI framework guards against the creation and spread of AI-generated child sexual abuse material (AIG-CSAM) and other sexual harms against children.

This presentation will cover the details of this initiative: how strategy has resulted in impact, how this framework for responsible and ethical AI as it relates to child safety has been adopted globally, and how AI governance and responsible AI professionals can pursue this same impact.

talks.title: Dr. Spencer Torene, Meibel: STAG: Structure Augmented Generation
talks.description:
Dr. Spencer Torene, Principal Research Scientist, Meibel

STAG: Structure Augmented Generation - Bridging Structured and Unstructured Data for Enhanced RAG Systems

Organizations today struggle with extracting insights from diverse data sources, often treating all content as unstructured even when inherent structure exists. We present STAG (STructure Augmented Generation), an innovative system that maximizes performance by automatically identifying and applying structure wherever possible within heterogeneous data collections.   STAG's core philosophy centers on structure-first processing. Rather than treating all content as unstructured by default, STAG identifies structural patterns and relationships that can be leveraged for enhanced retrieval performance. For content that remains genuinely unstructured, STAG creates both graph and table-based representations for discoverable entities in addition to creating traditional RAG embeddings. This dual structural approach applies organizational relationships even to unstructured content, ensuring that retrieval processes benefit from enhanced document context and interconnections.  At query time, STAG's structure-augmented approach delivers superior results by leveraging structured queries where applicable, semantic search where necessary, and automatically incorporating referenced documents through intelligent graph and table traversal. This structural foundation enhances RAG system performance by providing more precise retrieval, better context, and comprehensive responses.  STAG represents a paradigm shift from treating enterprise data as universally unstructured to intelligently applying structure at every opportunity. This approach unlocks significant performance gains in information retrieval and generation by working with data's natural organizational patterns rather than against them. The presentation will demonstrate STAG's architecture, showcase real-world implementation results, and discuss the system's impact on enterprise RAG performance metrics.

talks.title: Dr. Stella Umunna: Kill, Suspend, or Scale? Hands-On AI Governance with the CHOIR-G Framework
talks.description:
The Problem: Standard technical metrics like Accuracy and Recall do not measure real-world risk, especially in high-stakes environments. This workshop moves beyond theoretical AI ethics to provide a hard, quantitative framework for deployment decisions. Participants will learn the CHOIR-G Framework, a risk-weighted scoring model, and apply it in real-time to a notorious healthcare case study, calculating risk to make a definitive "Kill, Suspend, or Scale" deployment decision. As AI systems move from sandbox to production, engineering and leadership teams face a critical "AI Risk Gap." A model may boast high internal performance metrics, but if it fails in a live, dynamic environment, who is harmed? Who owns the risk outcomes? Are core error controls in place at reporting? This 90-minute workshop equips AI builders and strategists with the CHOIR-G Framework: a vendor-neutral, highly actionable governance methodology that bridges technical performance with social trust and enterprise accountability. CHOIR evaluates five core dimensions: Context, Human Impact, Organizational Accountability, Indicators, and Review & Oversight. Instead of passively listening to a lecture, attendees will be put to work. After a brief breakdown of the CHOIR-G mathematics : S = wC * C + wH * H + wO * O + wI * I + wR * R where: S = overall composite score wC = weight assigned to the C dimension wH = weight assigned to the H dimension wO = weight assigned to the O dimension wI = weight assigned to the I dimension wR = weight assigned to the R dimension C = score for the C dimension H = score for the H dimension O = score for the O dimension I = score for the I dimension R = score for the R dimension The room will break into groups to act as a board for governing enterprise AI. The Hands-On Case Study: Groups will be tasked with conducting a governance review of the Epic Systems Sepsis Early Warning System. In internal testing, the model boasted a high AUC-ROC, but in production, University of Michigan researchers (published in JAMA Internal Medicine) found it missed 67% of actual sepsis cases because the model "cheated" by picking up on when doctors were already ordering antibiotics. Given the life-or-death stakes, teams must debate the weights of each CHOIR dimension for this specific deployment, score the system's failure, and determine the necessary governance outcome, ultimately working through the process to establish the strict "Human-in-the-Loop" protocols required to secure such a system. What Attendees Will Walk Away Knowing: • The CHOIR-G Scoring Mechanics: How to implement a 1–15 risk-weighted scoring system for any AI model. • The "Critical 1" Automatic Intervention: How to establish non-negotiable guardrails in their deployment pipelines to prevent catastrophic edge-case failures. • Cross-Functional Translation: How to translate abstract ethical and risk concerns into concrete, quantifiable metrics that engineering, legal, and executive teams can agree on.

talks.title: Elliot Marx: Two Halves of Inference to Build, Eval & Run Agents
talks.description:
The AI stack is changing, but whether you’re building an agent or fine-tuning an LLM, the same problem remains: you need the right context to build, evaluate, and deploy reliable AI systems. Many failures that look like model or prompt problems are actually context problems, with agents making confident decisions that are inaccurate or based on stale data. Evals have the same context problem. If you evaluate an agent or fine-tuned LLM against non-realistic or incomplete context, you can’t know how it will perform on the tasks and data it will encounter in production. In this hands-on presentation, Chalk Co-Founder Elliot Marx will show how a unified context layer solves both. A context layer is the missing decision infrastructure to give live, governed data to agents and models at inference time - querying your data where it already lives, so every AI decision gets the real-time context it needs. The same system powers testing and evals, so you can prove that your agent is production-ready. With a context layer, you turn data that helps AI understand the world it’s acting on into agent context at the moment of inference - and run the full AI decision system. He’ll demonstrate the full workflow across use cases, from fine-tuning an open-weight LLM and serving it in your own cloud to testing an agent in a simulated time-bound environment with knowledge-cutoff data and tool access, evaluating against real-world tasks, and deploying in a sandbox. Finally, Elliot will share practical lessons from building context and infrastructure for ML and agentic systems used by companies like Whatnot, Turo, and Mission Lane, and a framework for making context and evals a core part of how you build AI.

talks.title: Emmanuel Ameisen | Keynote: Language Models, Inside Out: Finding world models hidden in the weights
talks.description:
Language models are superhuman text predictors. The best way to predict a piece of text is to build a rich model of the world that generated it. Look inside a language model and that's what you find: concepts shared across languages and modalities, plans formed well in advance of being enacted, and even evolved algorithms for arithmetic. Prediction, done well enough, becomes simulation. To guess the next word, the model learns to represent the hidden variables behind the text: a speaker's emotions, beliefs, and goals. The field of interpretability has spent the last few years decoding language model weights directly. This talk is a tour of some of the most important findings from this work, and of the mental model they add up to: a language model as a world model, hiding in plain sight in the weights.

talks.description:

A single task can fan out into hundreds of model calls, each carrying a repeated context prefix and adding latency that compounds across tool calls and reasoning steps. talks.title: Hai Guan: Right Query, Wrong Answer: Why AI Analytics Is So Hard, and How to Fix It
talks.description:
Every product team has an analysis backlog. Questions pile up, same metrics get re-sliced weekly, and when answers finally arrive, validation is manual and inconsistent. At many companies, the ratio is 80% execution mechanics to 20% actual thinking. We wanted the inverse. So we built AI Analyst - an open-source, multi-agent system powered by Claude Code that automates the full analytical workflow: from a business question to a validated, stakeholder-ready slide deck in roughly 30 minutes instead of days and weeks. What We built: The system orchestrates 18 specialized agents across a 4-phase pipeline - Frame, Analyze, Story, Deck - using DAG-based parallel execution. A Question Framing agent turns vague asks into testable hypotheses. Eight analysis agents run concurrently (descriptive, cohort, root cause, trend, validation, opportunity sizing). A Story Architect designs narrative beats before any chart is created - solving the "chart looking for a story" problem. A Chart Maker generates Storytelling-with-Data-styled visualizations with collision detection. Every output passes through 4-layer validation: structural, logical, business rules, and Simpson's Paradox checks, graded A through F. The system includes a knowledge layer that compounds over time: query archaeology captures proven SQL patterns, a corrections log ensures mistakes are never repeated, and organization-specific context (metrics definitions, business rules, team glossary) accumulates with use. It connects to any data source - CSV, DuckDB, Postgres, BigQuery, Snowflake. What I learned: The hardest part wasn't building the agents - it was getting an organization to trust and adopt AI-assisted analytics. Five real blockers emerged: security and legal approvals, data classification concerns, warehouse access, API cost ownership, and analyst skepticism. I'll share specific tactics for each, including the one that worked best: "show the output, not the pipeline." The critical design principle: AI can execute analysis fast, but it cannot tell you what question to ask or whether the answer makes business sense. We designed the system around human validation, not human replacement. The learning flywheel - run, review, spot errors, correct, store, improve - is what makes the system get meaningfully better over time. This talk is for data leaders, product managers, and engineers who want to democratize analytics without sacrificing rigor.

Video Recorded at The AI Conference. Copyright, The AI Conference, All Rights Reserved

talks.title: Hardik Nahata & Deepika Khera: Building Agentic AI at PayPal: Platform, Governance, and Agent Design
talks.description:
An agent that can act on production systems is a new actor in the enterprise. It has credentials, and it can accomplish complex tasks across systems autonomously. That changes what the platform underneath has to provide: identity and authorization for non-human actors, transaction-grade reliability, and observability that treats every agent action as a first-class audited event. At PayPal we run a fleet of specialized agents on shared infrastructure — agents that write code, deploy models, and monitor agents. They sit on a common substrate: a certified agent/mcp registry, agent-to-agent delegation, unified model routing under latency and cost pressure, enterprise memory that persists across sessions, and a governed skills layer so capabilities are reused rather than rebuilt. We're now extending that substrate across cloud project boundaries, so agents owned by different teams and deployed in different environments can find and delegate to each other. Once agents cross those boundaries, identity and audit become essential. In regulated financial infrastructure, governance, security, and Responsible AI aren't a layer bolted on, they're the substrate the swarm of agents runs on. This talk walks through that architecture, then gets into the parts that were hard to learn: graph-based orchestration with typed state contracts, how we scaled the agent orchestrator, normalizing two agent protocols into one response contract, human-in-the-loop at the right moments, and agent memory that survives across sessions. You'll leave with patterns you can apply to your own systems and a clearer view of the platform capabilities these systems rely on.

talks.title: Honpeng Guo, ByteDance: verl: A Flexible and Efficient RL Framework for LLM Reasoning & Tool-calling
talks.description:
Hongpeng Guo, Research Scientist, ByteDance

verl: A Flexible and Efficient RL Framework for LLM Reasoning and Tool-calling

Large language models (LLMs) have enabled advances in language understanding and multimodal tasks, yet scaling reinforcement learning (RL) with these models remains challenging: most existing frameworks either lack the abstractions needed to define and manage complex dataflows or cannot handle models with billions of parameters.
verl (https://github.com/volcengine/verl) is an open-source framework for building end-to-end RL pipelines with LLMs. It provides high-level abstractions and optimizations for dataflow orchestration and resource management via a Ray-based hybrid-controller model. It offers high-level abstractions for dataflow orchestration and resource management: the entire RL dataflow runs as a single controller process on the Ray driver, issuing primitive API calls to WorkerGroup modules. The WorkerGroup and ResourcePool components distribute computation and resources across GPU clusters, delivering high throughput and strong extensibility.
Since its release, verl has seen adoption in both academic research and industry production. It integrates with major training backends (FSDP, FSDP2, Megatron-LM) and inference engines (vLLM, SGLang), and supports various RL algorithms (PPO, GRPO, DAPO, etc) with effortless scaling. Recent trends in reasoning models bring new challenges to RL infrastructure, such as efficient tool calling, multi-turn interactions, and capability to scale up to giant MoE models like DeepSeek 671B. To lower the barrier to RL for advanced reasoning and tool calling, we recently improved verl with (1) efficient request level async multi-turn rollout and tool calling, (2) integration with expert parallelism for large scale MoE models, and (3) async system architecture for off-policy / async RL algorithms and flexible device placement.

talks.title: Ion Stoica, Berkeley: Reliability, an AI challenge
talks.description:
Ion Stoica, Professor & Executive Chairman, University of California at Berkeley, Anyscale

Reliability, an AI challenge

Reliability is a critical obstacle to the successful deployment of AI systems in production. As with conventional software, moving an AI system from prototype to production is far from trivial, requiring robust testing, debugging, and governance. However, unlike conventional systems where components have clear specifications, AI systems—particularly those built on large language models—are black boxes, making failures difficult to detect and diagnose. To address this challenge, we present two systems: LMArena, which evaluates LLMs with real human prompts to measure both accuracy and the impact of style, and MAST, a taxonomy and dataset that reveal why multi-agent systems fail, including poor specifications, misalignment, and weak verification. We argue that achieving reliability requires transforming AI development into a true engineering discipline, grounded in better specifications that are essential for building, debugging, and verifying modular and robust systems.

talks.title: Jeremy Adams: Experience Is Abundant. Knowledge Is Distilled.
talks.description:
Generative AI gave us an abundance of content. Agentic AI is giving us something potentially more valuable, while also much more overwhelming: experience. Every tool call, coding session, workflow, decision, observation, and robot trajectory leaves behind another trace of what happened, what worked, and what didn't. But accumulating raw piles of experience isn't the same as learning from it. This talk explores an emerging layer in AI systems devoted not simply to storing context, but to distilling experience into durable, reusable knowledge. We'll connect ideas appearing across agent memory, semantic layers, knowledge bases, coding agents, context graphs, and even physical AI: resolving repeated observations into entities, discovering relationships and patterns, turning trajectories into reusable skills, and feeding what we've learned back into future action. A number of knowledge primitives are competing for this layer, from the humble Markdown document and hypertext to vector embeddings, model weights, and knowledge graphs. Graphs, in particular, keep popping up. They may occupy a sweet spot: knowledge that is structured yet flexible, explicit and inspectable, portable across models and agent harnesses, and capable of generating other representations without surrendering the underlying structure. We'll pressure-test that claim, asking when the graph is useful, when it isn't, and whether increasingly capable models might eventually swallow the whole thing. The last wave of AI was about generation. The next frontier may be about accumulation: building systems that don't just produce more experience, but get better at distilling what it means.

talks.title: Jessica Li Gebert, Neudata: Data starved? Let’s feed the models

Jessica Li Gebert, Data Consultant, Neudata

Data starved? Let’s feed the models

“We’re running out of data” has become a common concern among AI developers. In this session, Jessica Li Gebert, data strategist at Neudata, challenges that perception - highlighting how data leaders are overlooking high-quality data assets stored behind corporate firewalls. This session is for AI developers who seek high-quality training data and organization that may be sitting on valuable datasets without a clear path to monetization. talks.title: Jonathan Nolen & Timothy Cook: Controlling AI Software Factories: Engineers in Charge at Agent Speed
talks.description:
AI is not just changing how fast software is written. It is changing how software is produced.  Engineering organizations are assembling agent-powered systems that write code, review pull requests, validate releases, deploy changes, and continuously improve production software around the clock, without human hands on every step. The promise of faster software delivery and continuous optimization is real. But as delivery becomes more autonomous, a new and more urgent problem surfaces: how do you stay in control of systems that never stop evolving? In this session, Jonathan Nolen, Chief Product Officer at LaunchDarkly, makes the case that the defining challenge of the AI era is not generating code — it is controlling autonomous systems in production. Traditional pre-production controls and the standard playbook of detect, fix, redeploy break down for agents that don't fail like traditional software. They drift. You can no longer catch issues before production. You have to control production. Jonathan will share what LaunchDarkly has learned building its own AI software factory — including what happened when coding agents met its oldest, most complex production code — and why every autonomous delivery system requires a closed control loop: observation, decision-making, intervention, and feedback, all running at runtime without a deploy cycle. Attendees will leave with a practical framework for building AI software factories that are genuinely fast and safe, and a clear answer to the question every engineering leader is now facing: when agents are doing the work, who stays in charge?

Video Recorded at The AI Conference. Copyright, The AI Conference, All Rights Reserved

talks.title: Joshua Rubin: Observe, Enforce, and Govern: The Fiddler Control Plane and Centor Models
talks.description:
An agent in your pipeline just wrote code, called an API, or touched a database, and nobody reviewed it first. That's the autonomy agents already have. The question is whether you'd know if one did something wrong, and how long it would take you to find out. That’s what the AI Control Plane is for: a system of trust that starts with evaluation, since that's what makes it possible to monitor an agent's activity, enforce policy on an agent's actions before they execute, and govern behavior across the agentic lifecycle. We'll show what this looks like in practice: inline guardrails that check an agent's actions before they execute, and dashboards that break down exactly what every agent is doing and spending by developer, team, and token. We'll also show how Fiddler Centor Models come batteries-included, no external API calls, no added cost per evaluation, so you can evaluate 100% of your traces or scale down to sampling for smaller deployments. The same approach works whether you're operating a handful of agents or a fleet. You'll leave with a practical way to decide which of your agents have earned more autonomy, and how to give it to them without losing the ability to govern what they're doing.

talks.title: Manqing Liu: Post-Training LLMs for Entertainment: Engagement, Safety & Non-Verifiable Rewards
talks.description:
Training LLMs for entertainment applications, such as AI characters and interactive storytelling, presents a unique opportunity: how to develop models that are engaging and safe. Measuring model responses is a specialization where there is not merely a set universe of objective criteria, as in other fields. As a result, we often use signals from user behavior, such as swipe interactions and whether a user continues the conversation or disengages, to infer preferences and guide model improvements. This talk will explore how we approach post-training in this setting using reinforcement learning with real-world user interaction data. We will discuss how to identify which user behaviors are meaningful and how to use them to improve models despite the lack of a clear ground truth. We will share practical techniques for balancing multiple goals. This includes methods for structuring training so the model learns from both positive signals (e.g., continued engagement) and negative signals (e.g., undesirable outputs), as well as strategies for prioritizing different objectives at different stages of training. We will also cover how testing and training models on difficult prompts helps uncover weaknesses and improve reliability in real-world use, and how improvements discovered in larger models can be transferred to smaller, more efficient models without sacrificing performance. Grounded in real-world implementation, this session will provide a clear framework for training and improving LLMs in domains where success is difficult to measure directly. Attendees will leave with practical approaches to working with imperfect user feedback, balancing competing objectives, and applying these methods to production AI systems.

talks.title: Nandini V.: No Agentic Sovereignty, No Agentic Security
talks.description:
For high-security organizations like government, finance, defense, and regulated industries, failing to secure agents isn’t just inconvenient. It’s catastrophic: stalled payments, delayed medical treatments, and dead power grids. More than 70% of regulated-industry leaders name security and privacy as their top barrier to adoption. Agents break the assumptions these industries were built on. Unlike deterministic software, they take actions on their own, reach into live systems, and act with privilege no one formally provisioned. The autonomy is the value. Where it acts, and on whose authority, is the exposure. The instinct is to bolt on data residency and call it solved. It isn't. Data sitting in a database is one thing; data an agent picks up, reasons over, and acts on is another—and that motion is where sovereignty actually breaks. In this session, we’ll detail why regulated industries need truly sovereign solutions to support agents in the environments where they run. We'll examine why data residency alone isn't enough, and unpack the risks across every sovereignty control point an agent touches—data, infrastructure, decision, and ecosystem Attendees will leave understanding the high-risk actions agents can take on their behalf, why probabilistic guardrails satisfy none of these dimensions, and what high-assurance controls — spanning identity, infrastructure, and decision authority—regulated industries actually need before they let agents act. Organizations that treat this as a continuous, auditable posture will be the ones who move fast in AI adoption and still pass the audit.

talks.title: Nathan Wallace: Actions speak louder than prompts: governing what AI agents actually do
talks.description:
Everyone is watching what goes into AI agents. Almost no one is watching what they actually do. The industry obsesses over the inbound boundary — prompt injection, guardrails, model alignment — while the real risk lands on the other side: the commands an agent runs, the data it moves, the credentials it reaches for, the systems it changes. An agent doesn't need to be jailbroken to cause damage; it just needs to be helpful in the wrong direction. Existing controls can't see this. Every tool in the security stack — secrets managers, DLP, identity, endpoint — watches a boundary: a vault checkout, a network egress, a login. Agents do their work, and their damage, in the space between those boundaries, where every action looks routine and the only identity in sight is a trusted human's. Prompts are too fuzzy to be controls; audit trails are precise but after the fact. Neither answers the question that matters: should this action happen, right now, in this context? This talk makes the case for a new layer: understanding each action an agent is about to take — what will run, what it will touch, and why — and evaluating it before it executes. I'll share real patterns of risky agent behavior from enterprise environments that are invisible to today's tooling. Whether you're enabling AI or governing it, you'll leave with a practical framework for the action layer — and the questions your current stack can't answer.

talks.title: Philip Kiely | Keynote: Beyond the Frontier: The economics of the multi-model era
talks.description:
For the last few years, the AI conversation has been dominated by a handful of frontier, closed-weight models but that era is ending. As open-source models have become better and better and new specialized model labs have emerged, the industry is shifting toward a multi-model future. This future is one where open source and closed-weight models are distributed, evaluated, and run side by side on shared infrastructure, and where the right model is chosen on quality and performance for a specific job rather than the lab who created it. Baseten sits at the center of this shift, serving as a hub for distributing both open source and closed-weight models at production scale. In this talk, Philip Kiely, author of Inference Engineering and early employee at Baseten, will make the case for why this shift is not just inevitable but good for the industry. The unit economics of open source models now dramatically outperform frontier models for equivalent tasks, and smaller, fine-tuned models frequently outperform large general-purpose models on quality, latency, and cost for real customer workloads. Drawing on data from production deployments, this talk will show why the future of AI isn't one model for all tasks. It's the right model, for the right job, at the right price.

talks.title: Piyush Agarwal: Introducing Redpanda's Agentic Data Plane
talks.description:
AI agents are increasingly deployed as digital employees—accessing enterprise data, making decisions, and acting autonomously. But agents are both less predictable than humans (prone to hallucination, misinterpretation, and adversarial manipulation) and more capable, with deep system access and machine-speed execution that can cascade damage fast. This makes it unsafe to trust agents to faithfully interpret or propagate security-critical metadata like access policies, data classifications, and behavioral constraints. We present Redpanda's Agentic Data Plane (ADP): an architecture using out-of-band metadata channels that carry security context, policy signals, and audit trails deterministically—entirely outside the agent's read/write path, across heterogeneous infrastructure. These channels enforce governance at every stage of the agent lifecycle: scoping data access going in, constraining actions during execution, and capturing tamper-proof audit trails coming out.

talks.title: Priyambada Jain, Black Rock: Agentic AI for Financial Data
talks.description:
Priyambada Jain, Senior Data Scientist, BlackRock

Agentic AI for Financial Data: Automating Insights from Large-Scale Tables

1. Problem Statement: Financial datasets are vast, complex, and difficult to process manually. Extracting key insights from large financial tables remains a bottleneck for analysts. Unlike free-form text, tabular data is hierarchical, relational, and context-dependent, requiring specialized techniques for accurate summarization and insight generation. Traditional LLMs struggle with numerical reasoning, row-column relationships, and multi-step financial calculations, making agentic AI architectures essential for structured data interpretation. 2. Agentic AI Approach: Built an autonomous AI agent leveraging LLMs and domain-specific fine-tuning to analyze, summarize, and extract key financial insights dynamically. 3. Core Capabilities:    a. LLM Fine-Tuning: Trained on financial documents to improve context understanding and numerical reasoning.      i. Bayesian Optimization for hyperparameter tuning.      ii.Contrastive Learning to improve structured data representation.      iii.Quantile Regression to enhance financial trend prediction.      iv. Expectation-Maximization (EM) for better handling of missing data in tabular structures. b. Named Entity Recognition (NER) & Ontology Learning:      i. Developed a NER model to learn the ontology of financial use cases, enabling precise identification of different columns and their        relationships.    ii. Fine-tuned an embedding model to capture semantic relationships between financial entities, improving contextual understanding        of structured data.   c. Evaluation Framework: Supports researchers in assessing different prompting techniques like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and Chain-of-Table (CoTab) to improve reasoning on structured financial data.    d. Tabular Data Extraction: AI pipeline identifies patterns, trends, and anomalies in financial statements.    e. Synthetic Data Generation: Capable of creating synthetic financial datasets for benchmarking, evaluation, and fine-tuning the framework.   f. Explainability & Auditability: Ensures AI-generated insights are traceable and interpretable for decision-makers.  4. Impact & Business Value:     a. Efficiency Gains: Reduces manual processing time from hours to minutes.     b. Enhanced Decision-Making: Empowers financial professionals with concise, data-driven summaries.     c. Scalability: Adaptable across different financial reports, including earnings statements, balance sheets, and regulatory filings. Conclusion: This agentic AI architecture bridges the gap between raw financial data and actionable intelligence, offering a research-friendly framework for advancing structured reasoning in AI. By addressing the unique complexities of tabular financial data, it enables more accurate, interpretable, and scalable AI-driven financial analysis.

talks.title: Robert Chiniquy: Agentic Memory, Logic, and Authorization
talks.description:
This talk introduces a specific, implementable architecture for context-aware agent authorization — using structured memory as a first-class input to the policy evaluation hot path. The core argument is that agent tool calls occupy a gap in the authorization model taxonomy. No single existing model handles them well: RBAC can confirm a user has a role that includes Jira access, but cannot scope a tool call to a specific project without creating a role per project. ABAC can evaluate request parameters against static constraints, but requires someone to have pre-configured those constraints — it doesn't know why project ALPHA is the right scope. ReBAC can traverse a relationship graph to determine that a user is related to project ALPHA through a team, but doesn't account for temporal context (the user was on ALPHA last quarter, now on BETA). The missing input is situational context: what is this user currently working on? What has their agent been doing in this session? What tools do people in this user's role typically use? The talk will present: A memory architecture designed for authorization — not general-purpose agent memory. Three typed stores (worker memory from identity/HR/project systems, agent session memory from conversation context, organizational baseline memory from usage analytics), each with different trust levels, update semantics, and confidence scoring. Temporal validity ranges on every fact for point-in-time audit queries. This draws on and synthesizes ideas from the academic agent memory literature (Zep/Graphiti for temporal knowledge graphs, Hindsight for belief evolution with confidence, MIRIX for typed multi-agent stores) but is purpose-built for the authorization use case. A write/read split architecture for the hot path. Memory facts are extracted asynchronously (tolerating LLM latency for fact extraction and confidence scoring). Authorization decisions are evaluated synchronously against pre-compiled facts using Datalog — deterministic, terminating, auditable, sub-millisecond. The evaluation does not call an LLM. It does not make network round-trips to external stores. The facts are local and pre-compiled. Memory-informed delegation policies. Concrete Datalog examples showing how a delegation can reference memory predicates instead of static parameter constraints. A rule that says "allow this Jira create_issue call if the target project is one the user is currently working on, per memory, with confidence above 0.7" — and if confidence is below the threshold, escalate to a human approval flow. Plus anomaly detection via organizational memory baselines: "this tool is not typical for this user's role" as a governance signal, not a hard deny. An honest treatment of the unsolved problems — particularly the local authentication and configuration barrier for non-technical users, and the challenge of governing memory itself (provenance, retention, review cycles) when memory facts influence authorization decisions.

talks.description:
Satyanandam Kotha, Staff Software Engineer, Uber

Distributed Real-Time Fraud Detection: A Scalable Architecture for Combating Fake Reviews in E-Commerce

This presentation introduces a cutting-edge distributed system for real-time fake review detection that addresses critical marketplace integrity challenges while delivering exceptional performance metrics. Our architecture leverages streaming data pipelines built on Apache Flink, Kafka, and Spark Streaming to process reviews as they arrive, enabling immediate identification of fraudulent activity with average detection latencies under 100 milliseconds—a substantial improvement over traditional batch-processing approaches.
The system employs a sophisticated hybrid detection model that combines natural language processing, graph neural networks, and behavioral analytics to identify complex fraud patterns. Our multi-model integration approach demonstrates a 0.94 precision score, significantly outperforming single-architecture alternatives that typically achieve 0.78-0.86 precision. The temporal pattern analysis component can detect coordinated campaigns involving as few as 8 accounts, with marked improvement in early detection rates compared to conventional methods.
For sophisticated collusion networks, our graph-based detection methodology achieves high detection rates for campaigns involving just 12 accounts—far exceeding non-graph approaches for similar operations. The system architecture scales near-linearly to 32 worker nodes with strong efficiency metrics, essential for processing massive review graphs containing 500 million to 3 billion edges.
Privacy and security remain paramount through our federated learning implementation, which achieves detection accuracy comparable to fully centralized approaches while dramatically reducing cross-organizational data exposure. Our differential privacy guarantees maintain F1 scores above 0.92 with privacy parameter ε = 4.6.
Production deployment across multiple e-commerce environments has demonstrated the system's effectiveness, substantially reducing fraudulent review prevalence while maintaining high availability. Resource utilization increases sub-linearly with traffic volume, and the system sustains low latency even at 5x normal traffic—critical for maintaining performance during promotional events when both legitimate and fraudulent review volumes typically spike.
This presentation will provide attendees with architectural insights and implementation strategies for building high-performance fraud detection systems that protect marketplace integrity and consumer trust.

talks.title: Simeon Bochev, Compute Exchange: AI is still killing innovation
talks.description:
Simeon Bochev, Co-founder & CEO, Compute Exchange

AI is still killing innovation

It sounds like a contradiction, but it’s not a suggestion that AI itself is doing the damage. Rather, it's the exponentially growing demand for compute – the raw infrastructure that powers AI – and the lack of equitable access to that essential resource. In other words: no compute means no innovation for far too many organizations, large and small. That has to change.
The system for buying compute doesn’t compute. Neither does the lack of market transparency, vendor lock-in, juggling multiple vendors, unused capacity, and heterogeneity. The reality is that most compute buyers are flying blind. There’s no real market price – access to the same GPU service can range from $1.58-$8.50 per hour. When a buyer is able to secure access, there’s no way of knowing whether or not it’s a good deal, or if the technology will even work.
This presentation will make the case for the commoditization of raw computing power, which could be transformative for fair and equal access. The innate properties of compute naturally lend themselves to standardization and liquid markets: Compute exhibits uniformity as AI's foundational infrastructure, much like electricity in power transmission. It represents an essential raw material for model development, commanding a massive market with capital expenditures in the trillions. Compute also demonstrates minimal differentiation in core capabilities across providers.
That’s why there’s a need for neutrality and a system that injects transparency and liquidity into the process. Simeon will make the case for a market that lets buyers access compute when they need it, while allowing providers to monetize unused capacity efficiently.

talks.title: Stephen Chin | Keynote: GraphRAG: The Definitive Guide - Patterns, Trade-offs & Production Systems
talks.description:
Download Stephen Chin’s book here: https://neo4j.com/books/oreilly-graphrag-definitive-guide/ GraphRAG has quickly become a catch-all term for everything from graph-enhanced retrieval to Text2Cypher, agent memory, and community-based summarization. That is exciting, but it also creates confusion. When people say “use GraphRAG,” what do they actually mean, and which pattern fits which problem? This talk gives AI engineers a practical map of the GraphRAG landscape. We start with the limits of vector-only RAG, especially when data is connected, multi-hop, dynamic, or needs to be explainable. From there, we break GraphRAG into a set of core building blocks: constructing knowledge graphs from structured and unstructured data, choosing among lexical, domain, and meta graphs, and applying retrieval patterns such as guided traversal, graph-filtered search, Cypher templates, Text2Cypher, graph embeddings, query-focused summarization, and agentic retrieval. The goal is not to present GraphRAG as one recipe, but as a toolbox with clear trade-offs. We will show when a lightweight pattern is enough, when a richer graph model pays off, and how to think about evaluation, governance, and production readiness from the start. Attendees will leave with a working mental model of GraphRAG, a taxonomy of the most useful patterns, and a decision framework for designing graph-powered GenAI systems that are accurate, explainable, and useful beyond the demo.

talks.title: Yuri Shelke: Scaling Enterprise RAG: Distributed Indexing and Dynamic Retrieval at Terabyte Scale
talks.description:
Standard vector search architectures collapse under the weight of indexing latency, ballooning storage costs, and degraded retrieval precision when enterprise RAG systems scale to terabyte-scale production knowledge bases, hitting a Scaling Wall. This session explores the engineering patterns required to build a high-throughput enterprise search infrastructure. Using our production implementation as a case study, we graduate from basic vector stores to a distributed indexing strategy. We will analyze the critical trade-offs between Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) accuracy and memory overhead, the impact of hybrid metadata-vector filtering on query latency, and the necessity of partitioned retrieval architectures to maintain sub-second response times. Attendees will gain a blueprint for a "Knowledge Lake" architecture, learning how to handle incremental indexing at scale, manage vector infrastructure costs, and implement dynamic query routing to ensure system consistency across distributed environments. Key Takeaways: * Distributed Indexing & Sharding: Partition billion-vector datasets across distributed nodes using HNSW/IVF algorithms to ensure sub-second retrieval without exhausting cluster memory. * Trade-off - ANN accuracy vs Memory: Tune ANN indexes for billions of vectors, balancing retrieval speed against infrastructure spend with tiered storage. * Partitioned Retrieval & IVF Strategies: Engineering strategies for segmenting vector space using Inverted File Indexing (IVF), centroid-based sharding, and cluster-level pruning to achieve high search completeness with minimal compute overhead. * Hybrid Filtering & Routing: Implementation patterns for combining structured metadata filters with vector similarity to optimize retrieval performance. * Operational Consistency: Monitoring ingestion lag, managing incremental indexing, and ensuring data integrity across distributed vectors. Engineering Trade-offs & Operational Insights: * Ingestion Scaling vs. Index Freshness: Dynamic task mapping in Airflow and Spark to parallelize the embedding bottleneck while managing vector database write-limits. * Vector Storage Economics: Reducing high-dimensionality embeddings cost through product quantization (PQ) and binary hashing. * System Resiliency: Handling retrieval hot spots and implementing circuit breakers for bulk data backfills that threaten to saturate vector endpoints.

talks.title: Zairah Mustahsan: Measuring What Matters: Statistical Rigor in AI Accuracy Evaluations
talks.description:
Most teams evaluate AI accuracy by running a handful of test queries, picking whichever system looks best, and shipping. The problem is that ad-hoc testing doesn't reflect production behavior and isn't replicable; worse, standard benchmarks aren't calibrated to specific use cases. When you're making infrastructure decisions that cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, cherry-picked demos are not a measurement strategy. This talk introduces a rigorous framework for evaluating AI search quality that applies classical ML statistical principles to a problem the industry has largely treated as subjective. I’ll cover how to construct a golden test set that actually predicts production performance, how to validate LLMs-as-judge against human raters before trusting them at scale, and how to run controlled comparisons across providers. The deeper argument is about what most evaluations get wrong at the measurement level. LLM-based evaluation is inherently stochastic, so the same query, run through the same system, produces different outputs across trials. Reporting accuracy alone can't tell you whether a performance difference is real or just noise; I’ll explain how to decompose evaluation variance into signal and instability. You’ll leave with a methodology you can apply immediately to your own vendor comparisons and internal eval pipelines.

Anthony Annunziata, Director of AI Open Innovation, IBM

Open Source AI:
Status, Opportunities, and Challenges from the Enterprise Perspective

talks.title: Dr. June Andrews, Lat Long Labs: Optimizing Quality of Life:A Feat of Brute Force and Ignorance
talks.description:
Dr. June Andrews, Founder, Lat Long Labs

Optimizing Quality of Life:A Feat of Brute Force and Ignorance

Lat Long Labs (LLL) presents the first of its kind – a platform for optimizing quality of life as a function of location and family. In this talk, we will dive into the technology enabling this breakthrough—a constraint optimization machine running over a multi-grid feature space that unifies hundreds of maps covering the eight dimensions influencing quality of life: wealth, employment, environment, health, education, recreation, community, and safety. These maps are personalized to family structure, zip code, occupation, and personal interests for all locations in the United States. All together, LLL produces one step closer to data science + machine learning + AI achieving the zenith of what tech can offer us: to optimize the quality of life for every family—every individual—every human heartbeat.

Optimizing quality of life is such a daunting task it can only be embarked upon with brute force and ignorance, until enough building blocks are in place for clever optimization algorithms to take over. LLL’s initial building block was the development of a personalized total tax model encoding thousands of tax laws. It was then augmented with a personalized income estimator and continually refined until achieving the first of its kind – a personalized discretionary income model – calculating generation of wealth as a function of family and location. Mastering personalized financial models is critical to making actionable recommendations. The additional seven dimensions similarly had models developed from basic building blocks to novel representations. Finally, using a technique from mathematical optimization, constrained optimization, good at handling high dimensional spaces with soft penalty functions, a global optimization is possible for quality of life as a function of location and family.

This talk introduces the architecture underpinning the first known model for simulating and optimizing quality of life as a function of location and family. From this model we show a series of case studies linking the theoretical results of the LLL model with real-life challenges and outcomes for families navigating the dynamic landscape of the United States.

talks.title: Dr. Samantha T. Arundel, U.S. Geological Survey: An Intelligent National Map
talks.description:
Dr. Samantha T. Arundel, Senior Science Advisor, National Geospatial Program, U.S. Geological Survey

An Intelligent National Map: Coordinating Structured Analysis and Scientific Validation Across Authoritative Geospatial Data

The U.S. Geological Survey’s National Map provides a consistent, authoritative foundation for elevation, hydrography, transportation, and land cover data across the United States. However, the increasing complexity of spatial problems has outpaced platforms built around static layer access or manual analysis. An Intelligent National Map (INM) is being developed as a modular framework that supports structured queries, coordinated model workflows, and transparent review of analytic results. Rather than serving as a single tool, an INM organizes existing federal datasets into reusable workflows that support spatial reasoning and policy-relevant analysis.
Each workflow is initiated through a user query and proceeds through configured steps for data retrieval, transformation, modeling, and review. All inputs are drawn directly from agency-maintained sources, including the 3D Elevation Program (3DEP), the National Hydrography Dataset (NHD), and land cover datasets such as LCMAP. Results are tied to specific records and returned with complete provenance documentation. Instead of replicating or warehousing data, an INM issues structured queries against live repositories using defined interfaces and schema constraints.
Workflows are carried out by task-specific agents, each aligned to a discrete operation such as model selection, input filtering, or threshold evaluation. Validation is handled by agents configured to compare analytic outputs to published values, ScienceBase records, or ontologically defined spatial relationships. For example, a workflow to delineate flood exposure may combine current stream gauge data with elevation derivatives and surface connectivity metrics to identify risk zones, which are then checked for agreement with hazard maps or published thresholds.
The platform supports use cases in hazard response, infrastructure planning, and environmental monitoring. Examples include wetland persistence mapping based on hydrologic connectivity, optimization of transportation alignments using topographic cost surfaces, and comparison of projected land cover scenarios for zoning evaluation. Results are returned as standardized spatial products along with intermediate diagnostics that document key parameter choices and processing steps.
Every analysis includes a structured explanation layer. Users can view variable contributions, input sources, and references checked by validation agents. Review modules simulate internal steps used in USGS publication workflows, including peer review and policy compliance checks. These are configured using synthetic review personas aligned to the USGS Fundamental Science Practices framework.
Initial development is focused on elevation and hydrography workflows where classification methods and source data are stable. Ongoing work includes refining query interpretation, extending validation loops, and establishing audit mechanisms consistent with governance guidance from the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. Long-term planning includes cross-domain integration and federation across federal organizations.

Building an Advanced Knowledge Assistant

A huge promise for LLMs is being able to answer questions and solve tasks of arbitrary complexity over an arbitrary number of data sources. talks.title: Jisheng Wang, Traceable: Securing the New Attack Surface
talks.description:
Jisheng Wang, VP Engineering and Head of AI/ML, Traceable

Securing the New Attack Surface:Navigating the Security Risks and Protection of LLMs

Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a cornerstone technology, reshaping every industry and revolutionizing how we interact with digital systems. Much like the advent of network computing and cloud technology before it, the widespread adoption of LLMs heralds a new era of innovation and, with it, a novel attack surface ripe for exploitation. This talk aims to shed light on the inherent security risks associated with LLMs with the real-world examples of LLM-targeted exploitation, and emphasize the importance of proactive threat management in safeguarding the future of LLM-driven applications. Since LLMs will be widely used in future applications, we will first give an overview of the Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Top 10 Application Risks and Top 10 API Risks which are still applicable to LLMs. Next we will focus on the OWASP Top 10 LLM Specific Risks, and delve into three detailed examples of Prompt Injection, Sensitive Information Disclosure, and Training Data Poisoning. Each example is accompanied by a demonstration of the potential for exploitation, and also the strategies for mitigating these threats and protecting against attacks.

The goal of this talk is to educate the broad AI developer community with the potential risks and vulnerabilities of LLMs and also the knowledge to protect against them, and foster a culture of security that keeps pace with the rapid advancements in AI technology.

talks.title: Kanika Narang, Meta: On-Device LLMs: Power of Conversational AI for Mobile and Wearable Devices
talks.description:
Kanika Narang, Research Scientist, Meta

On-Device LLMs: Unleashing the Power of Conversational AI for Mobile and Wearable Devices

Large Language Models (LLMs) have captured the attention of the tech world with their remarkable common-sense reasoning and generalizability. However, their large size and server transfer requirements can make them resource-intensive and slow, which is problematic for use in mobile or wearable devices like smart glasses and smart watches. Moreover, on-device computing could offer a solution to privacy concerns by keeping sensitive data, such as text messages or photos, on the device itself. To tackle these challenges, we’ve developed a more compact language model, ranging from 0.5B to 1.4B parameters. This model is designed to run on-device, providing a competitive performance for conversational grounded tasks, while also managing latency and memory usage effectively.

In this presentation, I’ll delve into our work on creating a versatile, on-device LLM, which is a distilled version of the LLAMA model, specifically tailored for conversational reasoning tasks. I’ll discuss our pretraining framework and our innovative approach to finetuning, which involves using LLM synthesized, task-specific data in a fresh dialogue format. Finally, I’ll share our strategy for scaling our text-based conversational model to a multimodal model, enhancing generative experiences such as composing text replies, document summarization, image captioning, and visual question-answering on wearables or mobile devices.

This talk will survey the role of sparsity in neural network computation, and the parallel algorithms and hardware features that nevertheless allow us to make effective use of it.

talks.title: Subhabrata Mukherjee, Hippocratic:Building the first Safety-focused Conversational AI for Healthcare
talks.description:
Subhabrata Mukherjee, Co-Founder and Chief Scientific Officer, Hippocratic AI

Building the first Safety-focused Conversational AI for Healthcare

Healthcare is facing a massive, global staffing crisis. The World Health Organization predicts a 10 million healthcare worker shortage by 2030, but stretched systems and underserved patients are already feeling the effects. Generative AI is the key to closing this staffing gap and ensuring more people can receive a level of care that has never existed before. With generative AI and large language models (LLM) working alongside healthcare workers of all kinds, we are looking to improve access, equity, and outcomes.

Hippocratic AI is building the industry’s first safety-focused LLM for healthcare, specifically focused on non-diagnostic, patient-facing, real-time healthcare conversation. We present Polaris — an agentic trillion-parameter constellation system with collaborative specialization and safety guardrails for human-like conversation. We will talk about the architecture, specialized training and alignment, and the first comprehensive clinician evaluation of an LLM system for healthcare with thousands of U.S. licensed nurses and hundreds of U.S. licensed physicians. We will also share industry use-cases to showcase the best and safest ways to deploy this technology, and explore what AI- and LLM-powered healthcare could look like in the future.

talks.title: Vipul Raheja, Grammarly: Text Revision with Large Language Models -- Challenges and Opportunities
talks.description:
Vipul Raheja, Applied Research Scientist, Grammarly

Text Revision with Large Language Models -- Challenges and Opportunities

Text revision is a complex, iterative process. It is no surprise that human writers are unable to simultaneously comprehend multiple demands and constraints of the task of text revision when producing well-written texts, as they are required to cover the content, follow linguistic norms, set the right tone, follow discourse conventions, etc. This presents a massive challenge and opportunity for intelligent writing assistants, which have undergone an enormous shift in their abilities in the past few years and months via large language models and human-feedback learning. In addition to the quality of editing suggestions, writing assistance has undergone a monumental shift in terms of being prescriptive systems to being human-feedback-driven, collaborative systems. However, writing assistants still lack in terms of their quality, personalization, and overall usability, limiting the value they provide to users.

In this talk, I will present my research, challenges, and insights on building intelligent and interactive writing assistants for effective communication and navigating challenges pertaining to quality, personalization, and usability.

Generative AI models and applications are being rapidly deployed across several industries, but there are several ethical and social considerations that need to be addressed. Prior to joining Amazon, he led similar efforts at the LinkedIn AI team, and served as LinkedIn’s representative in Microsoft’s AI and Ethics in Engineering and Research (AETHER) Advisory Board. Previously, he was a Researcher at Microsoft Research Silicon Valley Lab. Krishnaram received his Ph.D. in Computer Science from Stanford University in 2006. He serves regularly on the senior program committees of FAccT, KDD, WWW, WSDM, and related conferences, and co-chaired the 2014 ACM Symposium on Computing for Development.
